title: self-route-result
description: The coordinator's record of one self-route: a stage running again in place after a failure computed from what it produced — its agent process died, or it did not write a required output, or the required output at the run root is a previous attempt's, or the retry guidance it wrote was met in full by a retry its own verdict then failed — bounded by the budget its stage declares. Coordinator-written rather than stage-written, so it appears in no stage's schemas map and no agent is asked to satisfy it; the artifact exists so a run directory can say why a stage ran twice, rather than the reason living only in the re-run's prompt. A self-route spends neither retry_count nor max_retries, archives nothing under attempts/attempt-N/ and appends nothing to retry-history.json, so this file and the self-routed entry in execution-history.json are the whole of what it leaves. One is written per self-route under a name keyed by the stage, the attempt and the try, so no self-route overwrites another's. Optional fields are expressed by absence rather than by null, as clean-clone-result and execution-history do.

stage.description: The workflow stage that failed mechanically and is running again. A self-route has no destination other than itself, so this is both where the failure happened and where execution went.

attempt.description: The 1-based attempt this self-route happened within, unchanged by it: a self-route consumes no attempt number, so this matches the attempt of the rendered prompt the failed invocation was given and of any attempts/attempt-N/ directory of the same number.

try.description: The 1-based count of this stage's consecutive self-routes within this attempt, at or below the stage's declared max_self_routes. It is the same number the re-run's prompt filename carries as prompt-<stage>-attempt-N-try-M.md, so the prompt and this record can be read together.

failure.description: Which failure occurred. None of the four is a judgement about the work, which is why running the stage again is a plausible answer to all of them and why a boundary or schema violation is not among them. The first three are mechanical: the stage simply did not produce what it declared. The fourth, defective-retry-guidance, belongs beside them for the same reason rather than because it is mechanical — it is a fact computed from what the stage produced, that the retry guidance in force was met in full and the verdict failed the work anyway, so the guidance sanctioned the outcome it fails. Nothing there reads a guidance entry, an unmet reason or a blocking issue as language; the whole comparison is set equality over strings the verifier echoed. The fifth, suite-failed, belongs beside them on the same terms: the suite a stage declared, run by the coordinator as a subprocess after that stage's turn ended, exited non-zero. It is an exit status the coordinator owns rather than an agent's assertion about a run it made itself, and nothing reads the run's output for a count of tests or a list of failing names.

reason.description: The failure in the same words the escalation for it would have used, so a self-route and an escalation of the same failure name it identically.

statement.description: What the coordinator tells the re-running stage: why it is running again and, for the two failures that have one, which output was missing or stale. A failed agent process names no output — the invocation did not reach the point of declaring what it had done — and says instead that it exited without completing and that the working tree already holds whatever it wrote before it did. This is the coordinator's own statement and says so: a self-routed stage has no agent-authored guidance behind it, because no verifier saw the work.

artifacts.description: The artifacts the failure named, as the check reported them: the required outputs that were missing or stale, or — for a defective retry guidance — the artifacts the contradiction is between, the guidance that was met and the verdict that failed it anyway, or — for a failed suite run — the coordinator's record of that run and the path to its whole output. Absent for a failed agent process, which names none.
